issues.quote: It is an old joke in the house, and I would rather not repeat it now.
issues.fact: The fact sheet says only that the master said what he always says about the hall clock. It gives no joke, no habit, and no known offset.
issues.misreading: A solver could take the hall clock to be a known, deliberately mis-set joke clock, so its ten o'clock strike (regulator at 9:48) would be discounted as unreliable instead of being read as a plain reading.

issues.quote: I set its beat myself, most of it.
issues.fact: The fact sheet says nothing about who set the regulator or how much of it was set by whom. It says only that the regulator agreed exactly with the temple bell at ten.
issues.misreading: The phrase 'most of it' suggests someone else touched the regulator, which casts doubt on the regulator as the reference for the whole timeline and could lead a solver to distrust its 'twenty past ten' reading.

issues.quote: the kitchen clock, which is Rosa's American alarm clock
issues.fact: The fact sheet calls it only 'Rosa's clock'. It does not say what kind of clock it is.
issues.misreading: The 'American alarm clock' detail is new. A solver could infer a different movement or rate, or wonder whether 'the kitchen clock' is a separate fixed clock from the one the master held that afternoon.

issues.fact: The fact sheet says nothing about the watch inspection being an annual custom.
issues.misreading: The added yearly habit suggests the watch check was routine and possibly planned in advance, a whereabouts or timing hint the sheet does not give.

issues.quote: He meant it to speak at the turn of the century.
issues.fact: The fact sheet gives no repeater, no chime, and no 'turn of the century' date.
issues.misreading: A solver could read the phrase as a date clue, or take the repeater to be a clock whose chimes are part of the timeline, neither of which the sheet supports.

issues.quote: When you press the slide, it gives the hours in low notes. Each quarter is a doubled note. Then the minutes past the quarter come in high notes, one for each minute.
issues.fact: The fact sheet contains no repeater mechanism and no chime-decoding rule.
issues.misreading: This supplies a method for reading time from sound that the sheet does not give. A solver could use it to reinterpret any chime mentioned in the puzzle, which the sheet never states.
